newsitem.title: UK: POLL - London to see off rivals as financial hub.
newsitem.headline: POLL - London to see off rivals as financial hub.

text.p: London will maintain its position as the financial capital of Europe despite rival claims from other centres after the birth of a single European currency, a Reuters survey showed on Tuesday.
In the monthly survey of European economic and monetary union (EMU) expectations, 32 out of 40 contributors said they expected London to be Europe's principal financial centre in 10 years' time.
Main reasons cited by the contributors were the availability of a skilled workforce and a favourable regulatory environment.

"Even though modern telecommunications allow any bank effectively to operate from anywhere, at the end of the day it still needs well-trained and educated people to fill positions," said Brian Venables, senior bond strategist at ABN Amro in the Netherlands.
Only London's critical mass of talent would allow this, said Venables.

Only four supported Frankfurt as the future financial capital, and two predicted Paris would take the lead. One said it depended on whether Britain chose to remain outside EMU while one did not expect a clear leader.
Six contributors to the survey did not respond.
Respondents said Britain's easier tax regime and deregulation would maintain London's financial pre-eminence.
"The regulatory authorities in Britain are not averse to, and in fact have encouraged, innovation in new tradeable instruments," one contributor said.
Other reasons given were existing infrastructure, the entrepreneurial spirit and a language common with the United States.
"U.S. investors will continue finding an English- speaking country the best way to land in Europe," said Javier Requena, head of research and strategy at Benito & Monjardin in Spain.

Forty-six economists across the European Union contributed to the monthly survey carried out between July 11 and 14. The mean percentage chances of EMU starting on January 1, 1999 was 79 percent, the survey showed.

Most of those who expected London to hold its lead as a financial centre also expected Britain to join EMU a few years after launch. Frankfurt and Paris could gain eminence if Britain chose to remain an outsider.
"Then Frankfurt and Paris will become the two main financial centres," said Marc Touati, economist at Caisse Centrale des Banques Populaires in Paris.
"Paris will benefit from the modernity of its financial apparatus," he said.

If Britain stays outside EMU then the new European Central Bank (ECB), to be established in Frankfurt, would help the German government achieve its ambition to take over from London, contributors said.
Thirty-two out of 42 contributors said they expected London to maintain or strengthen its position as a major financial centre after the launch of the euro.
Ten said Britain's capital would lose its position.

Forty-one contributors said they saw Frankfurt holding or gaining status after January 1999, while just one, Padhraig Garvey of Riada stockbrokers in Dublin, foresaw Frankfurt losing business after the launch of EMU.
"Local markets in general, including Frankfurt and Paris, will see a shrinkage in wholesale activities such as bond and money market trading as the euro market moves to London," Garvey said .
Twenty-seven and 22 contributors respectively said they expected Paris and Brussels to maintain or strengthen their positions, while 15 and 20 expected them to lose out.
